# === docs/dns-hardening.md ===

# DNS resolver hardening — malformed-query requirements and test vectors

**Status:** requirements note for the DNS resolver in `eos`
(`eos/net`). eNet is a docs-only repo — the resolver does not live
here; this note is the contract its implementers and reviewers work
against. **Pattern source:** CVE-2015-5477 (ISC BIND, TKEY query
DoS, added to CISA KEV 2026-10-08): a single crafted query of an
unusual type reached an `assert` and killed the server. The resolver
equivalent for EoS is: **no wire input may assert, abort, panic, or
hang the resolver — malformed queries are dropped, never fatal.**

## Requirements

1. **Unknown or unusual QTYPEs are data, not errors of state.**
   A query for a type the resolver does not implement (including
   TKEY, type 249) is answered with an appropriate rcode (NotImp /
   FormErr) or dropped per local policy — it must never reach a
   code path that assumes the type is known.
2. **No assertion on wire-controlled values.** Header counts,
   label lengths, name compression pointers, and section sizes all
   come from the packet. Bounds are checked with ordinary error
   returns; `assert`/panic on any of them is a defect of the
   CVE-2015-5477 class.
3. **Compression pointers must terminate.** Pointer loops and
   pointers outside the packet are rejected; total name-expansion
   work per packet is bounded.
4. **Truncation is routine.** A packet shorter than its header
   claims, or cut mid-question/mid-record, is dropped whole — never
   parsed partially into resolver state.
5. **Oversized label chains are bounded.** Names are expanded
   against the 255-octet DNS limit; anything beyond is malformed
   and dropped, without allocating attacker-sized buffers.

## Test vectors (adopt verbatim as resolver tests in `eos`)

| # | Input | Expected behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Well-formed A query for a known name | Normal resolution (control) |
| 2 | Query with QTYPE = 249 (TKEY), otherwise well-formed | Rcode NotImp/FormErr or policy drop; resolver alive, next query (vector 1) still resolves |
| 3 | Query with QTYPE = 0 and QTYPE = 65535 | Same as vector 2 — no type is special-cased into a crash |
| 4 | Header claims QDCOUNT = 1, packet ends inside the question | Dropped whole; no state change; resolver alive |
| 5 | Question name is a compression pointer to itself | Rejected; expansion terminates; resolver alive |
| 6 | Compression pointer beyond the packet end | Rejected; resolver alive |
| 7 | Label chain expanding past 255 octets | Rejected as malformed; no oversized allocation |
| 8 | Response with ANCOUNT larger than the packet carries | Dropped; cache unchanged (no partial poisoning) |

"Resolver alive" in every row means: the process/task continues and
a following control query resolves correctly — the regression these
vectors exist to pin is a resolver that dies or wedges on the first
crafted packet.

## Relationship to the KEV gate

This note is the eNet-side disposition for the Oct 8 KEV batch's
BIND entry: the vulnerable component (BIND) is not in the org, but
the *pattern* — one crafted query type reaching an assertion — is
exactly what a small resolver must be tested against. The stack's
KEV doc records the component disposition; this note records the
pattern work.

# === docs/mqtt-broker-hardening.md ===

# MQTT broker hardening — spec and test vectors

## Scope

MQTT is eNet's device-messaging lane (bridges, telemetry,
fleet management). The broker-side code this note governs is
wherever an EmbeddedOS component accepts MQTT connections from
other devices — today that surface is small, and the time to
write its requirements down is before it grows. The pattern
this note defends against is the unauthenticated-broker class:
a broker that lets an unauthenticated connection reach
publish/subscribe state turns every topic it carries into an
open read/write channel, and brokers have repeatedly shipped
in exactly that configuration.

This is a spec for implementers, in the same shape as
`docs/dns-hardening.md`: numbered requirements, then a
test-vector table written so it can be transcribed into tests
verbatim.

## Requirements

1. **No session without authentication.** A CONNECT that
   carries no credentials — or credentials the broker cannot
   verify — is refused with the protocol's authorization
   refusal (MQTT 3.1.1 CONNACK 0x04/0x05; MQTT 5 reason code
   0x86/0x87) and the connection is closed. There is no
   anonymous mode in a shipped configuration; a build-time
   anonymous option, if one exists for bench testing, is off
   in release builds and its state is visible in the broker's
   startup log.
2. **Authorization is per-topic, not per-connection.**
   Authentication answers "who is this"; it does not make
   every topic writable. A client authorized for its own
   telemetry prefix cannot publish to another device's prefix
   or to broker-internal (`$SYS`-class) topics, and cannot
   subscribe outside its grant. Wildcard subscriptions (`#`,
   and `+` above the granted prefix) are refused unless the
   grant explicitly includes them — a wildcard is how one
   compromised device reads the whole fleet.
3. **Retained messages are publications.** A retained publish
   is stored and replayed to future subscribers, so it passes
   the same authorization as a live publish, and a zero-length
   retained publish (the retained-clear operation) is honored
   only from a client authorized for that topic.
4. **CONNECT floods are bounded before session state.**
   Connection attempts are rate-limited and half-open CONNECT
   handshakes time out in seconds, so a flood costs the
   attacker more than the broker; per-source and global
   pending-handshake caps are enforced before any session or
   subscription state is allocated.
5. **Oversized and malformed packets fail closed.** A packet
   header declaring a remaining length beyond the broker's
   maximum is refused without allocating the declared size;
   malformed fixed headers close the connection without
   affecting other sessions. (The same fail-closed discipline
   as `docs/dns-hardening.md` requires of the resolver.)
6. **Last-will messages are the client's own.** A will is
   published on ungraceful disconnect with the client's
   identity and only to topics the client could have published
   to itself; a will must never become a way to publish as
   someone else after disconnect.

## Test vectors

| # | Vector | Input shape | Expected broker behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| MQTTV-01 | Anonymous CONNECT | CONNECT with no username/password against a credentialed broker | Refused (auth refusal code), connection closed, no session state |
| MQTTV-02 | Wrong credentials | CONNECT with a well-formed but incorrect password | Refused as MQTTV-01; repeated attempts rate-limited |
| MQTTV-03 | Cross-prefix publish | Client granted `fleet/device-a/#` publishes to `fleet/device-b/telemetry` | Publish refused/not routed; connection state unchanged |
| MQTTV-04 | Wildcard overreach | Client granted `fleet/device-a/#` subscribes to `#` or `fleet/#` | Subscription refused for the out-of-grant filter |
| MQTTV-05 | Retained replay attack | Unauthorized client sets a retained message on a victim's topic, then a legitimate subscriber connects | Retained publish refused at publish time (MQTTV-03 rule); subscriber never receives it |
| MQTTV-06 | CONNECT flood | 1,000 half-open CONNECTs (no second packet) from one source | Pending-handshake cap + timeout engage; established sessions unaffected |
| MQTTV-07 | Declared-length abuse | Packet header declaring the maximum remaining length with a truncated body | Refused without proportional allocation; connection closed; broker serves other clients |
| MQTTV-08 | Will impersonation | Client A's will names a topic under client B's prefix | Will is not published on A's disconnect (or published only within A's grant) |

## Adoption

Whoever next touches an MQTT broker or broker-like component
in the org implements the vectors as tests named after their
ids (`MQTTV-01`…) alongside the code, the way `eos/net` is
expected to adopt the `DNSV-*` vectors from
`docs/dns-hardening.md`. If a conforming implementation
already exists for part of this surface, the adoption step is
still the vectors — run them, and record the result against
this note rather than re-litigating the requirements.

# === docs/device-bridges.md ===

# Device bridges: the agent-fabric hardware lane for eNet

The agent fabric's hardware-bridge lane gives AI agents real-device
reach — serial, MQTT, TCP, Modbus, debug probes — through MCP. Each
bridge below plugs into a specific eNet surface; the trust note is the
same everywhere, because bridges are network-facing by construction.

## The bridges

| Bridge | What it is | eNet surface it plugs into |
|---|---|---|
| **mcp2serial** (mcp2everything) | Serial-to-MCP bridge with Raspberry Pi Pico support | eNet's device story: agents talk to physical Pico 2s (pairs with the eos RP2350 board def `boards/rp2350.yaml`) |
| **mcp2mqtt** / **mcp2tcp** | MQTT/TCP device bridges | eNet's device story: the pub/sub and stream transports agents use to reach fleets |
| **modbus-mcp** | Modbus for industrial IoT | eNet's industrial angle: deterministic-comms lane (`docs/tsn-ethercat-lane.md`) extended to legacy industrial fieldbus |
| **embedded-debugger-mcp** (probe-rs) | Embedded debugging over MCP | Debug transport: flash/verify/inspect on real targets through the same fabric agents use for everything else |
| **xds110_mcp_server** | TI debug probes | The TI board queue: XDS110 probes as the agent-visible debug surface for TI targets |

## Trust notes (apply to every bridge)

Bridges are network-facing, so the eSec hostile-protocol posture
(`embeddedos-org/eSec` `docs/mcp-hostile-protocol-hardening.md`)
applies at each one:

- **Allowlisted destinations** — a bridge may only reach the devices
  and brokers it was configured for; discovery-on-the-network is off.
- **Identity binding** — devices authenticate to the bridge; the bridge
  authenticates to the gateway. No implicit trust because "it's on the
  bench."
- **Pinned versions + config-change approval** — the fabric's standing
  rules, per the 200k-stdIO-instances lesson.

## Relationship to the deterministic-comms lane

`docs/tsn-ethercat-lane.md` covers deterministic on-wire comms
(TSN/EtherCAT for the FRDM-IMXRT1186-class hardware). The bridges in
this document are the *agent-reachable* complement: TSN is how devices
talk to each other deterministically; the bridges are how agents talk
to devices at all.

# === docs/mcp-bridge-evaluation.md ===

# MCP bridge evaluation — mcp2mqtt, mcp2tcp, modbus-mcp

**Status:** evaluation (2026-10-13). This page evaluates three
MCP bridges against eNet's protocol surface and recommends a trial
order. The bridge lane itself — what each bridge is and where it
plugs in — is specified in [`device-bridges.md`](device-bridges.md);
this page does not restate it, it judges it.

## What is being evaluated

An MCP bridge puts a device protocol behind the Model Context
Protocol so an agent can reach real devices through the same fabric
it uses for everything else. The three candidates map onto eNet's
surface as follows:

| Bridge | Protocol | eNet surface | Fit for the device story |
|---|---|---|---|
| mcp2mqtt | MQTT publish/subscribe to a broker | eNet's MQTT device story: fleet telemetry, command topics | Highest. MQTT is the org's primary device-messaging surface; a bridge here reaches the most devices with the least new machinery, and the broker is a natural policy choke point. |
| mcp2tcp | Raw TCP streams to configured endpoints | eNet's TCP transport: legacy devices, bench instruments, stream protocols | Medium. Useful and simple, but raw TCP has no topic or session semantics — every safeguard (framing, auth, timeouts) is the bridge's own problem. |
| modbus-mcp | Modbus register/coil access | eNet's industrial angle (the TSN/EtherCAT lane's legacy-fieldbus complement) | High value, highest care. Modbus has no authentication by design and writes move physical equipment; the bridge is a safety boundary, not just a protocol adapter. |

## Provenance checklist (applies to every bridge)

No bridge is trialled, let alone adopted, until each row is answered
in writing — the eVera policy rules applied at selection time:

| Check | What "pass" means |
|---|---|
| Pinned source | The bridge's source is pinned to a specific commit in our configuration; "latest" is never a version. |
| Reproducible build | The pinned commit builds reproducibly in CI from source; no prebuilt binary blobs from the internet at run time. |
| Endpoint ownership | Every endpoint the bridge can reach is configured by us and allowlisted; the bridge cannot discover or wander to new endpoints on its own. |
| Credential isolation | The bridge holds device/broker credentials; the agent never does (below). |
| Read/write separation | Read and write tools are distinct, so write access can be granted (or withheld) per deployment. |

## Credential isolation — the broker rule

A bridge must be able to **broker credentials**: it pulls the broker
password, device key, or token from its own protected store at call
time and presents it to the device side, while the agent's side of
the conversation contains no credential material at all. Consequences:

- An agent (or a prompt-injection attack riding one) cannot leak a
  token it never held.
- Credential rotation happens in one place — the bridge's store —
  not in every agent configuration.
- Audit logs can attribute device actions to the bridge's identity
  and the requesting session separately.

A bridge that requires the agent to supply credentials per call
fails this check regardless of its other merits.

## Recommendation

1. **Trial mcp2mqtt first.** MQTT is eNet's main device surface, the
   broker gives a single policy and credential choke point, and the
   read/write split maps cleanly onto topic ACLs. Trial scope: one
   bench broker, read-only topics plus one non-safety write topic,
   credentials held only by the bridge.
2. **modbus-mcp second, read-first.** Trial with read tools only
   (register/coil reads against a bench PLC or simulator); write
   tools stay disabled until the trial report covers interlocks and
   failure modes for physical actuation.
3. **mcp2tcp last, bench-only.** Its lack of protocol semantics
   makes it the weakest fit for a general device story; trial only
   against a named bench instrument with a documented framing
   protocol.

A trial needs: the provenance checklist answered for the candidate,
a pinned deployment under the gateway, an allowlist containing only
bench endpoints, and a short trial report in this directory before
any production endpoint is added.

## Cross-references

- [`device-bridges.md`](device-bridges.md) — the hardware-bridge lane this evaluates.
- [`tsn-ethercat-lane.md`](tsn-ethercat-lane.md) — the deterministic-comms lane modbus-mcp complements.
- eSec `docs/mcp-hostile-protocol-hardening.md` — the hostile-protocol posture every bridge inherits.

# === docs/mcp-bridge-trial-plan.md ===

# MCP bridge trial plan — mcp2mqtt first, mcp2tcp bench-only

**Status:** trial plan (2026-10-16). This plan makes the trial
recommended by [`mcp-bridge-evaluation.md`](mcp-bridge-evaluation.md)
concrete: scope, safety shape, success criteria, and the exit
decision each trial informs. It adopts nothing — a bridge is
adopted only when its trial report says so, in writing, in this
directory.

## Scope

Two trials, in the evaluation's order:

1. **mcp2mqtt (first).** One simulated device behind mcp2mqtt,
   running against EoSim, publishing and consuming through one
   bench MQTT broker. Topic set: read-only telemetry topics plus
   exactly one non-safety write topic (the evaluation's trial
   scope). The broker requirements in
   [`mqtt-broker-hardening.md`](mqtt-broker-hardening.md) apply to
   the bench broker unchanged — the trial does not get a weaker
   broker than production would.
2. **mcp2tcp (last, bench-only).** One bench instrument behind
   mcp2tcp, against a stub endpoint with a documented framing
   protocol — no production endpoint, no discovery. Raw TCP has
   no topic or session semantics, so the trial exists to measure
   how much safeguard machinery the bridge itself must carry.

**Out of scope for this plan:** modbus-mcp. The evaluation
sequences it second and read-first (register/coil reads only,
write tools disabled until interlocks and failure modes for
physical actuation are covered). It gets its own trial plan when
the mcp2mqtt report is in.

## Preconditions

The evaluation's provenance checklist, answered in writing for
the candidate before the trial starts: pinned source commit,
reproducible build, endpoint ownership by allowlist, credential
isolation, read/write tool separation. A candidate that cannot
answer all five is not trialled.

## Safety shape

- **Allowlisted surface only.** The mcp2mqtt trial's topic
  allowlist and the mcp2tcp trial's endpoint allowlist are the
  whole reachable world of each bridge. Anything outside the
  allowlist is refused by configuration, not by agent discipline.
- **No unauthenticated bridge.** Both bridges run authenticated
  end to end. The lesson of the gateway auth-bypass class
  (CWE-290) applies to bridges exactly as to gateways: a bridge
  that lets an unauthenticated caller reach device commands is
  an open channel to physical equipment.
- **The agent never holds credentials.** The bridge brokers
  credentials at call time from its own protected store (the
  evaluation's broker rule); the agent side of the conversation
  contains no credential material, so there is nothing for a
  prompt injection riding the agent to leak.
- **Bounded commands.** Each trial defines its command set in
  advance; a command outside the set is a trial failure, not a
  feature request.
- **Teardown.** Ending a trial leaves no open listeners, no
  running bridge processes, and no credentials on the bench
  broker beyond its own store.

## Success criteria

Per bridge, all of:

1. The bridge's tools are listable behind the org's MCP gateway
   alongside the org's own servers.
2. A bounded command from the trial's command set executes
   against the simulated device (mcp2mqtt) or the stub endpoint
   (mcp2tcp), and its result returns through the fabric to the
   caller.
3. An out-of-allowlist request is refused by the bridge's
   configuration, with the refusal visible in the bridge's log.
4. An unauthenticated request is refused.
5. Teardown leaves the bench in the state the safety shape
   requires.

## Exit decision

Each trial ends with a short report in this directory recording,
per bridge: **adopt**, **defer**, or **reject** — with the reason
tied to the success criteria above and to the provenance
checklist. The decision is recorded in this plan's status line
when the report lands. Silence is not adoption: a bridge with no
report stays untrialled for planning purposes, however well the
demo went.

## Cross-references

- [`mcp-bridge-evaluation.md`](mcp-bridge-evaluation.md) — the evaluation and trial order this plan executes.
- [`device-bridges.md`](device-bridges.md) — the hardware-bridge lane both trials belong to.
- [`mqtt-broker-hardening.md`](mqtt-broker-hardening.md) — the bench broker's requirements for the mcp2mqtt trial.

# === docs/lorawan-study.md ===

# LoRaWAN study — native backend pattern + hardware-bridge pairing

> Status: research note, not a roadmap commitment. eNet has no code yet;
> the implementation lives in `eos/net/`. This note records what a
> LoRaWAN story for eNet could look like, following the pattern that
> landed in Zephyr 4.5.

## Why LoRaWAN for eNet

Matter/Thread covers the home; LoRaWAN covers the field — kilometers, not
meters. For eos-health-adjacent sensing (remote patient monitoring
gateways), eos-aero (ground-station telemetry), and eApps device targets
in agriculture/infrastructure, LoRaWAN is the long-range uplink that
Wi-Fi and Thread cannot be. It belongs in eNet's protocol landscape next
to the Matter/Thread note.

## The Zephyr 4.5 pattern (what to copy)

Zephyr 4.5 shipped a **native LoRaWAN backend**: LoRaWAN 1.0.x Class A
running directly on the LoRa radio driver (EU868), dropping the Semtech
LoRaMac-node dependency. The design lessons for eNet:

1. **Backend, not stack.** LoRaWAN is a MAC layer above the LoRa radio —
   structure it as a backend (`lorawan`) over eNet's radio abstraction,
   not as a separate stack. The radio driver owns the PHY; the backend
   owns join procedure, frame counters, ADR, and duty-cycle bookkeeping.
2. **Class A first.** Class A (uplink-driven, two short receive windows)
   is the lowest-power, widest-supported class — the right default for
   battery sensors. Class B/C are follow-ups, not day-one.
3. **Region as configuration.** EU868 vs US915 vs AS923 differ in channels,
   duty cycle, and dwell time — make the region a build-time config with
   the channel plan as data, not code branches.
4. **No Semtech dependency.** The old approach (LoRaMac-node as an
   external component) is exactly what Zephyr removed. A native backend
   keeps the security story (eSec: key storage for AppKey/NwkKey) inside
   the org's audit boundary.

## What eNet would need

- A `LoRaMac` backend in `eos/net/` implementing join (OTAA), confirmed/
  unconfirmed uplink, and the Class A receive windows.
- Region channel-plan data files (EU868 first — the Zephyr-validated one).
- Key provisioning story: AppKey/NwkKey via eSec key management, never
  baked into firmware images in the repo.
- Duty-cycle enforcement in the backend (regulatory, not optional).

## Hardware-bridge pairing (agent fabric)

For the device story, two MCP bridges from the agent-fabric plan pair
naturally with eNet protocols:

- **cramen/modbus_connector** (Sept 2026, `--read-only` flag) — the
  best-maintained Modbus MCP server. Modbus/TCP gateways are how
  industrial LoRaWAN network servers expose device data; a read-only
  bridge lets agents poll registers without write risk.
- **mcp2mqtt** — LoRaWAN application servers (ChirpStack, TTN) speak MQTT
  on the application side. An mcp2mqtt bridge gives agents the downlink/
  uplink topic surface for device management.

Pattern: radio/MAC in firmware (`eos/net/`), application-server
integration via MCP bridges — the same split as the KB plan's
docs-MCP/tools-MCP separation.

## Open questions

- LoRaWAN 1.1 security context (Join Server split) vs 1.0.x simplicity —
  the Zephyr backend chose 1.0.x; follow unless a deployment needs 1.1.
- FUOTA (firmware update over LoRaWAN) fragmentation story — deferred,
  but the eBoot update path should know the MTU constraints exist.

# === docs/matter-thread-note.md ===

# Matter / Thread landscape note (KB seed)

> Status: research note, not a roadmap commitment. eNet has no code yet;
> the implementation lives in `eos/net/`. This note records what eNet's
> commissioning story would need if/when Matter support is pursued.

## Why Matter matters for eNet

Matter is the application-layer standard the smart-home industry converged
on. For an embedded OS with health- and home-adjacent ambitions (eos-health,
eApps device targets), speaking Matter is table stakes for "works with"
ecosystems (Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings).

## The stack, bottom-up

| Layer | Technology | eNet relevance |
|---|---|---|
| Radio | 802.15.4 (Thread), Wi-Fi, Ethernet | Link technologies eNet already claims |
| Mesh | Thread 1.3/1.4 | Needs a Thread stack — OpenThread is the reference |
| Commissioning | BLE (Matter commissioning) | Every Matter device commissions over BLE first |
| Application | Matter (application clusters, data model) | Needs the Matter SDK or a subset |
| Security | PASE/CASE session establishment, DAC attestation | Ties directly to eSec (key management, attestation) |

Key point: **Thread is not a Matter alternative — it is Matter's
low-power transport.** A "Matter over Thread" device uses BLE to get
commissioned, then operates over the Thread mesh. eNet cannot do Matter
without both a BLE story and a Thread story.

## Silicon worth watching

- **ESP32-H2** — 802.15.4 + BLE 5 (LE); Espressif's Thread/Zigbee vehicle.
  No Wi-Fi: a pure 15.4 end-device chip.
- **ESP32-C5** — 802.15.4 + Wi-Fi 6 + BLE; the first Espressif chip that can
  be a Thread end-device *and* a Wi-Fi Matter device in one SKU.
- **nRF54 series** (Nordic) — Thread + BLE + Matter SDK support is Nordic's
  home turf; relevant if eNet ever targets Nordic silicon.

## What eNet's commissioning story would need

1. **BLE commissioning bearer** — Matter commissioning happens over BLE
   (GATT). eNet's BLE link layer must support the commissioning window
   (advertising the discriminator, GATT service for PASE).
2. **Thread stack** — OpenThread port for at least one 15.4-capable target
   (ESP32-H2 is the natural first target). This is the biggest lift.
3. **Border router story** — Thread meshes need a border router to reach IP
   networks. EoSim could simulate one before hardware exists.
4. **Device Attestation (DAC)** — Matter requires a Device Attestation
   Certificate chain at commissioning. That is eSec's domain (key
   provisioning, certificate storage); eNet and eSec must design this
   together.
5. **Application clusters** — start with On/Off + LevelControl (lights),
   the smallest certifiable surface, before sensor clusters.

## Suggested sequencing (if pursued)

BLE link → OpenThread port (H2) → simulated border router in EoSim →
PASE/CASE via eSec → minimal Matter application (on/off light) →
certification pre-test. Each step is independently shippable and testable;
do not attempt the full stack at once.

## References

- Matter specification — Connectivity Standards Alliance
- Thread 1.4 specification — Thread Group
- OpenThread — https://openthread.io (Apache-2.0)
- Espressif ESP-Matter SDK — the fastest path to a working demo on H2/C5
- eSec — Device attestation and key management (co-design required)

# === docs/subghz-three-way-plan.md ===

# Sub-GHz three-way plan

Date: 2026-10-07. Sibling to `docs/lorawan-study.md` and
`docs/matter-thread-note.md`.

## The three lanes

Sub-GHz IoT is splitting into three standards lanes, and eNet needs a
position on all three:

1. **Wi-Fi HaLow (802.11ah)** — long-range Wi-Fi for IP-native sensor
   networks; simplest application-layer story.
2. **Thread Sub-GHz** — Thread's 802.15.4 radio moved down from 2.4 GHz;
   Mesh over IP for smart-home/industrial.
3. **Zigbee "Suzi"** — the CSA's brand for 802.15.4 sub-GHz (EU 868 /
   NA 915 MHz). Certification opened in 2026; already shipping in products
   (pierregode/ragnar, Sept 26).

## The design question: coexistence

HaLow and Suzi share the same 868/915 MHz bands. Running both stacks on one
device — or in one deployment — is not a free lunch. Required before eNet
commits to a dual-stack story:

- **Duty-cycle accounting** per band/region (EU 868 has strict duty-cycle
  caps; NA 915 has dwell-time rules).
- **Channel planning** so HaLow's wider channels don't deafen Suzi/Thread
  reception.
- **Interference testing in EoSim** — simulate the mixed-band environment
  before it is built (pairs with the M5Stack SX1262 radio platform def).

## Watch: Apple Oct 13

Apple's Oct-13 home-hub event is expected to cover smart-home hardware and
LG-built Thread/Matter accessories. If Apple ships Thread as the default
home radio, the **Thread Border Router story becomes table stakes** for any
eNet smart-home positioning. Revisit this doc after the event.

# === docs/tsn-ethercat-lane.md ===

# The deterministic-comms lane: TSN + EtherCAT

**Status:** direction (2026-10-08). eNet's wireless work (LoRaWAN study,
Matter/Thread note, sub-GHz three-way plan) covers the IoT edge. This
document opens the *deterministic* lane: Time-Sensitive Networking and
EtherCAT for industrial control, robotics, and onboard-AI flight
systems -- where "best effort" is not an option.

## Why now: named hardware

Two October 2026 boards make this lane concrete instead of aspirational:

- **NXP FRDM-IMXRT1186** -- M7 @ 800MHz + M33 @ 300MHz, **dual GbE TSN**
  plus 2x Fast Ethernet for EtherCAT/TSN, motor-control headers. One
  board carries both the TSN endpoint and the EtherCAT master story,
  plus the motor it would drive.
- **Upbeat Bluemag Pi** -- SiFive E3 (flight-critical) + E2 (AI/system)
  RISC-V flight controller with onboard AI, demoing at CEATEC Oct 13-16.
  Onboard-AI flight control needs deterministic comms between the
  real-time core and the AI core -- exactly the TSN use case.

## Lane scope

| Layer | eNet position |
|---|---|
| TSN endpoint (802.1AS time sync, 802.1Qbv scheduling) | Planned; FRDM-IMXRT1186 is the reference target |
| EtherCAT master | Planned; same board, 2x Fast Eth |
| CAN FD | Noted (Arduino VENTUNO Q carries it; the robotics lane overlaps) |
| Deterministic inter-core comms (dual-brain boards) | Design input from Bluemag Pi / VENTUNO Q |

## Non-goals

eNet does not implement a full TSN switch stack on day one. The lane
starts at the *endpoint*: time sync + scheduled transmission on the
reference board, with the switch-side work explicitly out of scope
until an endpoint ships.

## Watch items

- **CEATEC Oct 13-16**: Bluemag Pi demo -- watch for published
  latency/jitter numbers on the E3/E2 split; they become eNet's
  reference budgets.
- **Apple Oct-13 hub event**: Thread/Matter watch (separate lane, but
  the hub is a TSN-adjacent time-sync story for the home).

## Hardware anchor: i.MX RT1186 TSN switch profile

The FRDM-IMXRT1186 is not just a TSN *endpoint* board — the i.MX RT1186
carries **dual Gigabit Ethernet with TSN switching** in silicon, plus two
Fast Ethernet ports for EtherCAT/TSN. That makes it the bridging-model
reference for the lane, not only the endpoint reference.

**Bridging model.** The on-chip TSN switch sits between the two GbE MACs:
time-aware shaping (802.1Qbv) and time sync (802.1AS) apply at the switch
ports, so scheduled traffic keeps its latency budget *across* the bridge,
not just on the wire. The two Fast Ethernet ports hang off the same
switching fabric for the EtherCAT/TSN segment — one board can bridge a
TSN backbone to an EtherCAT cell.

**eNet surface mapping.**

| eNet surface | RT1186 mapping | Lane phase |
|---|---|---|
| TSN endpoint (802.1AS, 802.1Qbv Tx) | Either GbE MAC as endpoint | Now — the lane's day-one scope |
| TSN bridge/switch | On-chip TSN switch, dual GbE | Later — explicitly out of scope until an endpoint ships |
| EtherCAT master | Fast Ethernet ports | Planned, same board |

**Trust note (per the eSec posture).** A bridge is a privileged position:
it sees every frame. The bridge path boots fail-closed — the switch
configuration is part of the measured boot chain (eBoot #162 envelope
thinking applied to network config), and a bridge that cannot attest its
config does not forward. An unattested switch is a wiretap with a
datasheet.
